slides.title: HypertensionPersistent B/P of 140 mm Hg (Systolic) and 90mmHg (Diastolic)
text: HypertensionPersistent B/P of 140 mm Hg (Systolic) and 90mmHg (Diastolic)
Most people who have hypertension are symptom free
May later see clinical complications such as:

slides.title: Essential (Primary) Hypertension:
text: Age, tobacco, alcohol, obesity, family history, stress
Elevated B/P with an identified cause
Cirrhosis, endocrine disorders, renal disorders, pregnancy

slides.title: Hypertension Management
text: Increase knowledge of disease process and lifestyle changes and medications to control hypertension
Rebound hypertension – when abruptly stopping medications
Compliance with treatment plan – side effects to drugs are usually temporary
What is the client at risk for if they stop their medications?

slides.title: Recommended initial drugs include diuretics, beta blockers or both
text: Recommended initial drugs include diuretics, beta blockers or both
Give diuretics first – then adrenergic inhibitors second

slides.title: Thiazide Diuretics – chlorothiazide (Diuril), hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ)
text: Increases excretion of Na and H20
Mild side effects – dry mouth, thirst, weakness, drowsiness, lethargy, muscle aches and fatigue, tachycardia, GI disturbance
Postural hypotension may be potentiated by ETOH, hot weather or other drugs – opioids or barbiturates
Encourage high potassium rich foods (i.e., fruits)
Contraindicated in gout, allergy to sulfonamides

slides.title: Loop diuretics – furosemide (Lasix), bumetanide (Bumex)
text: Blocks reabsorption of NaCL and H20 in kidney
Used when thiazides fail or need rapid diuresis
Contraindicated in gout; allergy to sulfonamides
Side effects: thirst, N/V, skin rash, postural hypotension
Contraindicated in renal and liver failure
Side effects – drowsiness, lethargy, HA, diarrhea, skin eruptions, urticarial

slides.title: Adrenergic Inhibitors – reserpine (Serpasil), methyldopa (Aldomet), clonidine (Catapres), prazosin (Minipress)
text: Adrenergic Inhibitors – reserpine (Serpasil), methyldopa (Aldomet), clonidine (Catapres), prazosin (Minipress)
Impairs synthesis & reuptake or depletes stores of norepinephrine
Causes venous pooling, decreased venous return, decreased cardiac output, pulse rate; sedation and drowsiness
Calcium Channel Blockers  - nifedipine (Procardia), diltiazem (Cardizem) and verapamil(Calan)
Decreases afterload and slow conduction of AV node
Decreases peripheral vascular resistance by inhibiting enzyme which converts Angiotension I to Angiotension II

slides.title: Beta blockers – propranolol (Inderal), metoprolol (Lopressor), nadolol (Corgard)
text: Blocks sympathetic nervous system – slows heart rate and lowers blood pressure
Often used together with vasodilators to allow reduction in dosage of both agents
Check apical pulse and B/P before administering
Remember learn the drug categories and common endings!!!!!!
Acts on smooth muscle of blood vessel , direct vasodilator
Check apical pulse and B/P before administering

slides.title: Coronary Artery Disease
text: Narrowing of coronary arteries by atherosclerosis
Results in ischemia and infarction of the myocardial tissue
One of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality

slides.title: Angina
text: Episodes or paroxysms of pain or pressure in  anterior chest
Insufficient blood flow d/t atherosclerosis in coronary arteries
Reduced blood flow and O2 to myocardium, resulting in sensation of chest pain
Eating a large meal, emotional, sexual activity, cold

slides.title: Types of Angina
text: Stable Angina –chest pain relieved with rest or nitroglycerin
Unstable Angina – progressive increase in episodes of pain; occurs at rest
Variant angina (Prinzmetals Angina)    vasospasm induced, not related to activity, occurs most often at rest
Silent ischemia – no angina but objective evidence of ischemia on EKG or w/ stress test

slides.title: Client Education
text: Avoid OTC drugs that increase heart rate/blood pressure – nasal decongestants, diet pills
Use stool softeners to avoid constipation. Straining during a BM (Valsalva) should be avoided.
Avoid stress – decreases myocardial O2 consumption

slides.title: Medications
text: What labs do we monitor for heparin or enoxaparin?
What is the antidote for heparin? Enoxaparin?

slides.title: Nitroglycerin
text: Common dose – NTG 0.4 mg (1/150 gr) SL every 2-5 minutes x 3 PRN
Inactivated by air, light, heat, moisture, time

slides.title: Nitrate Preparations
text: Tell family where med is kept
Inform dentist and other physicians that you are taking vasodilators
- One tab under tongue every 5 minutes x 3 tabs
Sit 15-20 minutes after taking tablet to prevent dizziness, faintness, discomfort
Do not give NTG if BP<90 systolic
Take 3-5 minutes before activity known to trigger an attack, such as exercise or sexual intercourse
can NOT be taken with nitrates?

slides.title: Nitrate Paste and Patch
text: - Non-hairy proximal anterior arms, thighs, chest,
Paste should be kept tightly closed, stored in cool place
– chest preferred, inner arm, rotate sites
- Do not apply to distal extremity
- Apply new one patch if falls off
- May remove 12-24 hours to prevent tolerance

slides.title: Immediate Action if Pain Not Relieved by NTG
text: Immediate Action if Pain Not Relieved by NTG

slides.title: Common Diagnostic Testing for Angina
text: Stress Testing – determines hearts response to increase demand for O2, screens for ischemic heart disease, determines functional capacity of heart post-MI
Pre-test preparation-NPO x 4 hours, avoid stimulants (tobacco and caffeine); wear sneakers and comfortable clothing; explain procedure
Procedure – continuous heart and O2 saturation monitoring during stressful exercise (treadmill or bike) to attain a target heart rate
Post-test care – monitor heart rate and B/P 10-15 min. till returns to baseline

slides.title: Common Diagnostic Testing for Angina
text: Pharmacologic stress testing – dipyridamole (Persantine) or adenosine (Adenocard) IV in lieu of exercise to attain target HR
May cause temporary flushing or nausea; test  lasts
Mimics effects of exercise by maximally dilating coronary artery
S/E– chest discomfort, HA, flush, nausea, dizziness
Pre-test – no theophyllines 24-48 hours prior, no eating/drinking 4 hours before, no caffeine, chocolate, carbonated drinks; hold Persantine if prescribed

slides.title: Common Diagnostic Testing for Angina
text: Evaluates blood flow thru aorta, coronary arteries and right and left heart chambers
NPO 8-12 hours, shave prep insertion area

slides.title: Common Diagnostic Testing for Angina
text: Procedure – catheter inserted into femoral or radial artery; 1-2-hour procedure; hard table; cold room
Post-care – pressure dressing to insertion site, keep leg still x 4-6 hours
Supine with leg straight and HOB no more that 30 degrees
Assess distal pulses; CMS checks to leg
May turn side to side; assess for bleeding
Fluids to flush dye from system
Help to get up 1st time – orthostatic hypotension
Discharged same day or next day; shower only (no tub bath)
Discharge – ASA, beta blocker, NTG, ACE inhibitor

slides.title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty (PTCA)
text: Atheroma's that occlude at least 70% of lumen of major coronary artery
Conditions that do not respond to medical treatments
Pts with lesions of left main coronary artery not candidate
Improves blood flow within a coronary artery by “cracking” atheroma w/ inflated balloon on end of a catheter

slides.title: Coronary Artery Stents
text: Woven stainless steel mesh provides structural support; maintains patency
Placed over an angioplasty balloon – when balloon is inflated mesh expands & presses against vessel wall
Better results if PTCA and stent
Eventually endothelium covers the stent and it is incorporated into the vessel wall
On ASA lifetime to prevent thrombus
May be on Plavix up to one year after

slides.title: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG)
text: Revascularization of myocardium when angiography and stent ineffective/unacceptable treatment
Coronary arteries are usually at least 70% occluded
Blood vessel grafted beyond lesion of occluded blood vessel
Saphenous vein, internal mammary artery, radial artery, gastroepiploic artery

slides.title: Minimally Invasive Direct Coronary Artery Bypass
text: Minimally Invasive Direct Coronary Artery Bypass
Coronary artery bypass done w/ minimally invasive technique
May or may not be on bypass system

slides.title: Myocardial Infarction
text: Reduced blood flow in coronary artery d/t atherosclerosis
Complete occlusion of  artery by embolus or thrombus
Vasospasm- sudden constriction or narrowing of coronary artery causes decreased O2 leading to necrosis
Decreased oxygen supply-from acute blood loss, anemia or hypotension
Increased demand for oxygen-from rapid heart rate, thyrotoxicosis of ingestion of cocaine

slides.title: MI Chest Pain
text: MI pain begins suddenly w/o cause, persists hours to days not relieved by rest or NTG
Signs and symptoms of MI cannot be distinguished from those of unstable angina
Other body responses include SOB, pallor, diaphoresis, clammy, cold, dizziness, N/V, shock (sympathetic response to severe pain)

slides.title: TIME IS MUSCLE – used to indicate urgency of appropriate treatment to improve client outcome
text: TIME IS MUSCLE – used to indicate urgency of appropriate treatment to improve client outcome
Give thrombolytic within 6 hours of chest pain onset
Permanent damage to area of myocardium scar formation in area of injury

slides.title: ECG within 10 minutes of admission to ED
text: ECG within 10 minutes of admission to ED
Evaluate for cardiac cath or thrombolytic therapy
Alteplase (t-PA, Activase), IV heparin or Lovenox, clopidogrel or ticlopidine, glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor
Upright position and 2 IVs need placed

slides.title: Myocardial Infarction
text: EKG – Within 10 minutes of arrival to ED changes may be seen in 2-12 hours  (may take 72-96 hours)
T wave –enlarged for 24 hours then inverts within 1-3 days for 1-2 weeks
ST segment –elevation in epicardial damage, depressed in endocardial damage ; first to return to normal (1-6 weeks)
Q wave – large wave within 1-3 days; usually permanent

slides.title: Serum Cardiac Markers
text: Elevates in 4-6 hours, peaks 10-24 hours, return to baseline in 10-14 days
Always increased in severe angina, coronary insufficiency & AMI
Isoenzymes specific to location of greatest concentration myocardium – MB,
Release begins 1hr after MI, peaks in 18 hours
Serial testing traces degree of ischemia/injury

slides.title: Serum Cardiac Markers
text: Protein found in cardiac and skeletal muscle; helps to transport O2
Starts to increase within 2 hours, peaks within 3-15 hours
Negative test is an excellent parameter for r/o  AMI; + test doesn't indicate MI
First test result is negative, repeat in 3 hours  *Another negative test confirms that client did not have an MI

slides.title: Complications of an MI
text: Cardiogenic shock  - may occur after massive MI
Untreated, has an over 90% mortality rate
Interventions: Trendelenburg position, Dopamine drip, Foley, IV
PE - due to immobility & venous stagnation
What is the most common complication after a MI?

slides.title: Lanoxin (Digoxin)
text: Improves contractility, decreases HR, decreased speed of conduction
Low potassium enhances action of digoxin!!!
Hold and notify HCP if less then 60
What is the antidote for digoxin?

slides.title: Heart Failure
text: Dysthymic heart rate, murmur extra heart sounds S3

slides.title: Heart Failure
text: Client may be placed on a low sodium diet
Client may have a fluid restriction

slides.title: Care of Feet and Legs
text: Extra socks in winter, with larger shoes
No heating pads, whirlpool or hot tubs
Call MD if any skin breaks
No iodine or alcohol to the skin
Trim nails straight across after showering

slides.title: Deep Vein Thrombosis
text: Treat with anticoagulants and antiplatelet meds
Do NOT assess using the Homan’s sign!!!!

slides.title: Recurring inflammatory process of the small and intermediate vessels of (usually) the lower extremities
text: Recurring inflammatory process of the small and intermediate vessels of (usually) the lower extremities
Most often occurs in men ages 20-35
Progressive occlusion of vessels results in pain, ischemic changes, ulcerations, and gangrene.

slides.title: Raynaud's Disease
text: Intermittent arterial vaso-occlusion, usually of the fingertips or toes
Sudden vasoconstriction results in color changes, numbness, tingling, and burning pain
Episodes are usually brought on by a trigger such as cold or stress.
Protect from cold/other triggers. Avoid injury to hands/fingers.

slides.title: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
text: Intense & persistent pain described as tearing or ripping
Pallor, diaphoresis, tachycardia, falling BP, 50–75% mortality
Must be surgically treated before it ruptures!!!

slides.title: Valves
text: Unable to fully open (stenosis) or fully close (regurgitation)
Prophylactic antibiotic therapy prior to dental procedures, surgery, childbirth

slides.title: NGN NCLEX-RN Question
text: The nurse has taught a client who has hypertension and a body mass index of 28. Which of the following statements by the client would indicate a correct understanding of the teaching?
“I should limit my sodium intake to 3300 mg per day.”
“I will participate in a maximum of 1 hour of exercise per week.”
“I can drink the maximum of 3 beverages that contain alcohol per day.”
“I am going to eat less calories per day by following the Mediterranean diet.”
